title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: A model only knows what's in its prompt. Retrieval is the mechanism that decides, out of everything you could put there, which pieces actually get in, by searching, not by hoping the right chunk made the cut.
objectives: Explain why retrieval exists: the gap between "in the prompt" and "known by the model"
Describe what an embedding is and why cosine similarity measures relevance, not magnitude
Explain the role of a minimum-relevance threshold, and why "closest available" isn't always "relevant"
Implement cosine similarity and top-k retrieval over a small in-memory document set

hints.title: Hint 1: conceptual
hints.mdx: Break it into two pieces: a helper that scores one query vector against one document vector, and a second step that scores every document, filters, sorts, and slices. Don't try to do all four at once in one loop.

hints.title: Hint 2: specific
hints.mdx: Cosine similarity of vectors a and b: dot product divided by (magnitude of a times magnitude of b). Dot product is the sum of `a[i] * b[i]` across matching indices. Magnitude is the square root of the sum of each vector's own squared components (Python's `math.sqrt`).

hints.title: Hint 3: near-solution
hints.mdx: If either magnitude is 0 (a zero vector), return a score of 0 immediately for that pair, don't divide by zero. After scoring every document, filter out anything with `score < min_score`, sort the rest descending by score using `sorted(..., key=..., reverse=True)`, then slice with `[:k]`.

tests.name: Results are ranked by similarity, exact match scores highest and sorts first
tests.hint: Sort your scored documents descending by score. The document with vector [1,0] against query [1,0] should score 1.0 and come first.

tests.name: Cosine similarity ignores vector magnitude (scale-invariant)
tests.hint: Divide the dot product by the product of both vectors' magnitudes. [1,0] and [5,0] point the same direction, they should both score ~1.0 against a [1,0] query, regardless of length.

tests.name: min_score excludes low-relevance documents even when k allows more
tests.hint: Filter out any scored document with score < min_score BEFORE slicing to k. Document B (opposite direction, score -1) should be excluded when min_score is 0, even though k=5 would otherwise have room for it.

tests.name: k limits output to the top-k highest scores, regardless of input order
tests.hint: Score every document first, then sort the FULL scored list descending, THEN slice to k. Slicing before sorting (or sorting the wrong direction) gives the wrong top-k.

tests.name: A zero-length document vector scores 0 and never raises or produces NaN
tests.hint: Before dividing by the product of magnitudes, check if either magnitude is 0. If so, return a score of 0 for that pair instead of dividing by zero.

questions.question: Query vector \[1, 0\] compared against document vector \[0, 5\]. What's the cosine similarity?

numeric.correct: Correct. [1,0] and [0,5] are perpendicular, cosine similarity is 0.
numeric.incorrect: Not quite. [1,0] and [0,5] are perpendicular (90°), cosine similarity of perpendicular vectors is always 0.

questions.question: Query vector \[3, 4\] compared against document vector \[6, 8\] (same direction, double the length). What's the cosine similarity?

numeric.correct: Correct. [6,8] is exactly [3,4] scaled by 2, same direction, so cosine similarity is 1, magnitude is irrelevant.
numeric.incorrect: Not quite. [6,8] points in the exact same direction as [3,4] (it's just scaled by 2), so cosine similarity is 1.

questions.question: Why does cosine similarity divide out vector magnitude instead of just using raw dot product as the score?

options.text: Because magnitude reflects the vector's length, not how semantically related the underlying texts are
options.why: Dividing out magnitude leaves a pure measure of direction, which is what corresponds to semantic similarity.

options.text: Because dot product is too slow to compute for large vectors
options.why: That's not the reason, dot product is actually a component of cosine similarity itself, and isn't meaningfully slower. The issue is what raw dot product means, not how fast it runs.

options.text: Because raw dot product can never be negative
options.why: Raw dot product can absolutely be negative, for vectors pointing in opposing directions. That's not the reason magnitude gets divided out.

questions.principle: Dividing out magnitude leaves a pure measure of direction, which is what corresponds to semantic similarity.

questions.question: A retrieval system with k=5 and no minimum-score threshold is asked a question totally unrelated to anything in its document collection. What does it return?

options.text: Its 5 best-scoring documents anyway, even though none of them are actually relevant
options.why: Without a minimum-relevance threshold, top-k always returns k results, whatever scored highest, relevant or not.

options.text: An empty result set automatically, since nothing matches well
options.why: Not automatically, top-k without a threshold has no concept of 'not good enough,' it always returns exactly k results (or fewer if the collection has less than k documents), ranked by whatever scored highest, relevant or not.

options.text: An error, since no document scores above a reasonable relevance level
options.why: No error, similarity scoring doesn't know what 'reasonable' means without an explicit threshold, it just returns the mathematically highest-scoring k documents.

questions.principle: Without a minimum-relevance threshold, top-k always returns k results, whatever scored highest, relevant or not.

questions.question: A RAG system retrieves 3 chunks (400 tokens total) for a query, then sends them plus the user's question (50 tokens) to a model with an 8000-token context window and 1000 tokens reserved for output. Using Module 2's terms, is this call anywhere near the input budget limit?

options.text: No, it's well under budget: 450 tokens used against a 7000-token available input budget (8000 window − 1000 output)
options.why: 400 (chunks) + 50 (question) = 450 input tokens, against a 7000-token available budget, plenty of headroom.

options.text: Yes, it's already over budget since retrieval adds tokens on top of the question
options.why: 450 total input tokens is far below the 7000-token available input budget, adding retrieved chunks does add tokens, but this specific call is nowhere near the limit.

options.text: It's impossible to tell without knowing the exact tokenizer used
options.why: This course's planning estimate (or any reasonable estimate) is precise enough here, 450 tokens against a 7000-token budget isn't a borderline case that needs exact tokenizer precision to evaluate.

questions.principle: 400 (chunks) + 50 (question) = 450 input tokens, against a 7000-token available budget, plenty of headroom.
